meta.title: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.description: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.hed: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.dek: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.headerImg: wnba-framed.png | The WNBA logo hung inside an empty gilt picture frame

content.value: I love basketball and have loved it all my life, but I only became a WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm.) Now I’m kind of obsessed.
Since then, I’ve also become fixated on a question. Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA, too?

fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy | A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026. Their hottest topics: literal war and women’s basketball.
This question dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue came at a family gathering. I was chatting with an older conservative family member, who, out of the blue, started name-dropping WNBA players, saying praiseworthy things about superstar Caitlin Clark and suspect things about other Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, my Google Chrome app recommended more WNBA news. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News.
Wait, what?
I saw dozens of Fox News takes on women’s basketball, often with a clear political bias, and an implicitly racist and homophobic framing.

January 2025 | green | WNBA star ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) who ==hurt== Caitlin Clark's ((Caitlin Clark|face)) eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies
May 2025 | pink | Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese ((Angel Reese|face)) a jacka-- for jealousy of Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in response to ESPN analyst

content.value: Headline after headline pit the league’s most famous straight white star, Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.
All this perplexed me. So I began to collect data. How does Fox News cover the WNBA differently than everybody else?

content.value: Why does Fox News talk about Carrington, Cloud, and Griner so much?
DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner

It’s political. These players’ vocal leftist views—on race, gender, BLM and more—make them a target for conservative coverage of the WNBA, which has long sought to frame the league as both dangerously radical and illegitimate.

For example, Carrington has publicly criticized Clark for not being vocal enough in denouncing her racist and bigoted fans. She has fouled Clark and Cunningham in high-profile ways. And she’s made it clear that she doesn’t like Trump.

content.value: Cloud’s outspoken activism—for BLM, Gaza, trans rights, and more—has also been a focal point. Meanwhile, Griner was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, making her a consistent subject of news. But she is often criticized for her progressive views, too. And it’s no coincidence that these are all queer Black women.

This is cable news coverage of the WNBA, via their chyrons—you know, those headlines that appear at the bottom of your screen.
Fox News talks incessantly about hard fouls and hits against Clark. This is a kind of dog whistle, as I will explain below.

content.value: In summer 2026, the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

In July, Sophie Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face)), the Fever’s shooting guard, made openly anti-trans remarks. While she told ESPN that she had gotten “negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that," she also expressed a desire to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." Later, she doubled down on these comments, which inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her—including Vice President J.D. Vance and infamous TERF J.K. Rowling.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

According to recent reports, Fox News spent more than 13 hours talking about the WNBA this summer. Even their own pundits are confused—and exhausted—by this excessive focus. As commentator Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

value.caption: Jesse Watters on The Five, August 2026.

content.value: How did professional women’s basketball—a league that, for decades, most people didn’t watch or care anything about—transform into a mainstream political lightning rod?

It didn’t happen overnight. And the media, especially conservative media, played a key role. So let’s dive into the data and see how Fox News has framed the WNBA as a hot-button culture war issue—one that was primed, at the right moment, to explode.
The Data

To contextualize this summer’s events, I wanted to get a broad view of Fox’s WNBA coverage, and I wanted to examine how Fox talks about the WNBA, not just how often. So I collected any Fox News article (both headline and full text) that mentioned the WNBA or its players over the past six years. This includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox.
As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

Additionally, I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.
The Timeline
For most of its history, Fox News barely covered the WNBA. They talked about the NBA much more.

value.caption: Mentions of Caitlin Clark in Fox WNBA articles

content.value: You can see that coverage clearly surges in the “Caitlin Clark era”—that is, after Clark was drafted into the league in April 2024.
Both before and after Clark, though, Fox News put an ideological spin on their women’s basketball reporting. One way they’ve achieved this is through a reliable cast of characters.
The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe
Fox News often speaks the most loudly through the voices they platform, allowing them to express extreme views without direct blame.
What’s more, Fox often pits players against each other, seeking to amplify divisive political narratives.
Let’s look at the web they’re been spinning.

content.value: Rejecting “Identity Politics”—But Not Really
Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in its WNBA coverage.

Recently, Bobby Burack, writing for Fox’s Outkick, criticized ESPN for being “racial idolaters” in their reporting about Clark. He called out the narrative that Clark is only a star “because America has starved for a straight white girl to save them from a league of largely black LGBTQ women.” He continued:

That narrative is not supported by the history of superstardom in American sports. Yet it has shaped ESPN's coverage from the start… ESPN ought to add some diversity to its WNBA commentary—diversity of opinion, that is.
Here’s the irony. When it comes to the WNBA, Fox News talks about race, gender, and identity more than any other outlet—and about twice as much as ESPN.

content.value: Across all the outlets, discussion of race and racial justice peaks in 2020. This is true for Fox, too.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and lock arms during a moment of silence in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP

In 2020, WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of BLM. They walked off the court during the national anthem and wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television. They also successfully campaigned for Democrat Raphael Warnock to win a U.S. Senate seat, defeating Atlanta Dream co-owner Kelly Loeffler, who was loudly opposed to players’ activism. The players demonstrated that they had real political power.
All this was frequently covered by Fox, and often framed in implicitly disapproving terms.

Enter Caitlin Clark
In 2024, Clark—the three-point phenom from Iowa—was drafted #1 in the WNBA. And the culture war debates really heated up.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Clark’s popularity has drawn millions of new viewers and fans to the league. Many commentators have noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal.
It is undeniable that Clark has drawn in a whiter, more conservative, and more mainstream audience than the WNBA—a historically Black and queer league—has had in the past.
why-does-left-hate-clark-fox.png
everything's-racist-fox
Fox News has been obsessed with dispelling the identity-related dimension of this narrative.

At the same time, Fox News has played up Clark’s treatment in the league, specifically hard fouls committed against her, often in implicitly racialized terms that malign the Black and/or queer players who committed the fouls.

steps.text: Case in point: Fox News has consistently discussed “hard” fouls against Caitlin Clark more than other outlets.

steps.text: They also invoked race and racism more than other outlets, as well as culture war buzzwords like “privilege.”

content.value: Who Gets Framed How?
Trans Women in Sports

Fox News consistently fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war. They denied that race, sexuality, or gender were relevant considerations in the league, yet foregrounded them more than any other outlet.

The implicit misogyny, and suspicion of “social justice” and queer communities, laid the groundwork for the right-wing, anti-trans movement to rise up and seize the WNBA as a central issue—even though no trans women currently even play in the league.

value.caption: Fox WNBA articles per month that mention trans athletes or eligibility in women’s sports. Source: Fox News.

steps.text: Through 2025, Fox planted the seed for controversy around trans issues and the WNBA, discussing it periodically but consistently.
Then, in 2026, it exploded.
And as a share of everything Fox writes about the WNBA, trans coverage went from a sliver to the majority: in August 2026, nearly two out of every three Fox WNBA articles mention trans athletes.

content.value: Among the TV networks, Fox News talks about trans issues way more than the others.

content.value: As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” Watters said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agenda.

Sports are political. They have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platform to advocate for justice. Players in the WNBA are a great example. But we should be wary of how narratives about the WNBA are being framed by the right-wing media and outside parties who have little to no actual investment in the league.

When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. It was completely different from every other (men’s) professional sporting event I had ever been to. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to recognize this framing—and push back against it—lest we all get played.
Data and Methods
I collected WNBA articles from Fox News, ESPN, Yahoo Sports, Just Women’s Sports, The Athletic, CBS Sports, and USA Today.
The chyrons come from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye project.
The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
